You're responding to a comment where I wrote that I would never use Xen with an argument not to use Xen. All I'm saying is that "formal verification", at least as it exists in current systems, is not why I wouldn't use Xen.

> the formally-verified configuration of seL4 doesn't actually do much

As a systems security engineer myself I would disagree and know several others that would as well. All depends on your circles, applications, and threat model I suppose.

Xen, Hyper-V, and KVM have all had major security flaws in the form of logic violations, spacial memory corruptions, use-after-free, and pointer corruptions that allowed hypervisor trust boundary violations. I expect most if not all of those classes of bugs could have been prevented by formal verification.

Xen likely has a bad reputation with both of us because of a history of preventable flaws like these.

In my applications every single daemon gets its own sandbox, which is a VM whenever possible. Some with network, some without network, different filesystem and vsock access for maximum damage control and minimal trust between daemons. The hypervisor is the most important security boundary to me especially when isolating user-controlled workloads. The more confidence I can get that it is correct the better.

Like some of what I'm saying is just that if you tell a systems security person "we're using seL4 because of its formal verification", you're going to get eye rolls. Whatever else you want to say about it, the formally-verified configuration of seL4 doesn't actually do much, meaning whatever system you're building on top of it is going to be where all the security drama is anyways.

I'm certainly not telling you to use Xen. I wouldn't use Xen for anything untrusted.

I for one do not want any code in the TCB that is not formally verified, tiny, and easy to audit with every line of code justified.

SeL4 is the only open, mature, and formally verified L4 solution I am aware of that can run on modern servers, but IIRC given vCPUs are not first class objects and any low level CPU virtualization features are handled in user space, it comes at a real performance cost making it only suitable for single-core or non-performance-critical applications.

Nova by contrast was built to handle the expensive and trust critical TPM and vCPU handling directly for high performance remotely attestable multi-core applications without having to reach for something as heavy as Xen, though formal verification is admittedly not as complete as SeL4 yet AFAICT, though lots of recent progress here.

Those are pretty big tradeoffs, but if you or anyone else knows other viable xen alternatives this general shape with a tiny easily-auditable footprint, please chime in!

Most of the L4s have hypervisor situations. I don't know about TPM support. Generally the vibe I get from systems security people is a bit of eye-rolling about the formal verification of things like L4; the real win is just drastic attack surface reduction.

And then, of course, L4s live in millions and millions of shipped products, which is a reason to consider L4 instead of something novel, but I'm not saying you should or shouldn't.

Is there a well tested L4 hypervisor solution with hardware accelerated virtualization and raw TPM support formally verified to a similar or greater level than Nova with similar remote attestation and security features?

SeL4 is the closest contender on my radar atm.
Yep, very similar, but L4 is a little bit more general purpose (despite being microscopically tiny) and a little more battle-tested.
Nova is L4 inspired, and interchangable with L4 kernels in Genode.
I don't know much of anything about Nova but since the late 1990s this has also been the pitch for L4; there are several mature L4's.

I am more convinced by the day that the Nova Microhypervisor approach is correct.

Do virtualization with a tiny formally verified microkernel and have complex kernels like Linux run underneath instead of letting a huge, complex, and brittle linux kernel and vm ecosystem control the hypervisor layer.

children.text: That’s fascinating. I’ve seen this sort of thing on protocol implementations in layer 4+ but it’s rare to find it in layer 3.

The actual vulnerability got very little discussion. It's clever. Because Linux networking people are obsessed with checksum performance, virtio-net plumbs checksum offload metadata through the host/guest driver interface. Guests can thus deliver the host packets along with instructions on what to checksum. The vulnerability is a missing sanity check that allows checksum instructions to instruct the host to overwrite the header length field in the IPv4 header, rather than the checksum field.

Crucially, this happens in the middle of packet processing, so the kernel code is forced to work with two different ideas of how long the IPv4 header is. All hell predictably breaks loose.

children.text:
I was reading through and thought "surely I missed a step here" in more than one place.

They mention in part 1 having a write primitive that can hit a 64 byte region, but never really explained how that worked. I'm guessing this was them being able to have checksum offload write TCP/UDP checksum values into the overhang region past the valid data. Maybe the memory map was set up that way, but obviously relies on getting really lucky with getting their page table in the next page after their packet.

Also it was never called out, but as far as I can tell their exploit should only be able to target the beginning of pages for reading/writing. In order to rug-pull the socket logic that reads the IP IHL field, the IP header content needs to be in a page mapped to the guest. The only useful way to use this attack is to have the region spill out of the guest page into whatever page comes next in the kernel's memory map. (Which also makes the mentioning of the skb linear header kind of confusing, since that would be in a completely unrelated kernel memory region, and just have the data pointers pointing into their data, which is what happens for zero-copy network drivers, which presumably was set up for the kvm network for them to retain guest control over the packet.)
